questions.question: The Edwardian Period began in January 1901 following the death of Queen Victoria and the accession of:
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria died in January 1901 and was succeeded by her eldest son, King Edward VII, who reigned until May 1910.

questions.question: Although King Edward VII died in 1910, the Edwardian literary period is conventionally extended until the outbreak of:
options: The Second Boer War in October 1899
The Irish Civil War in June 1922
The First World War in August 1914
questions.explanation: Literary historians conventionally extend the Edwardian era from 1901 to the outbreak of World War I in August 1914.

questions.question: Which trio of prominent novelists epitomized Edwardian social realism and the critique of English class and material life?
options: Charles Dickens, William Thackeray, and Anthony Trollope
Aldous Huxley, Evelyn Waugh, and Graham Greene
Kingsley Amis, John Wain, and Alan Sillitoe
H. G. Wells, Arnold Bennett, and John Galsworthy
questions.explanation: Wells, Bennett, and Galsworthy were the three leading Edwardian realist novelists examining English social institutions.

questions.question: Which Irish-born dramatist and Fabian Socialist turned the Edwardian stage into an arena for debating social and moral issues?
questions.explanation: George Bernard Shaw dominated the Edwardian theatre with witty plays of ideas inspired by Henrik Ibsen and Fabian socialism.

questions.question: Which 1903 four-act philosophical comedy by George Bernard Shaw includes the famous third-act dream sequence 'Don Juan in Hell'?
questions.explanation: Shaw published 'Man and Superman' in 1903, dramatizing his philosophy of the creative Life Force and Don Juan in Hell.

questions.question: In George Bernard Shaw's play 'Major Barbara' (1905), the idealistic heroine Barbara Undershaft serves as an officer in:
questions.explanation: In Shaw's 1905 comedy 'Major Barbara', Barbara is a major in the Salvation Army whose father manufactures munitions.

questions.question: In George Bernard Shaw's comedy 'Pygmalion' (1912–1914), who is the Cockney flower girl trained in phonetics by Henry Higgins?
questions.explanation: In Shaw's 'Pygmalion', phonetics professor Henry Higgins bets he can pass off Cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle as a duchess.

questions.question: Which Edwardian novelist and dramatist began his famous 'Forsyte Saga' family chronicle with 'The Man of Property' in 1906?
questions.explanation: John Galsworthy published 'The Man of Property' in 1906 as the opening novel of 'The Forsyte Saga'.

questions.question: In John Galsworthy's 'The Man of Property' (1906), which possessive solicitor is the central 'man of property' of the Forsyte clan?
questions.explanation: Soames Forsyte embodies upper-middle-class possessiveness, treating both art and his wife Irene as personal property.

questions.question: Which 1910 naturalistic tragedy by John Galsworthy exposed the cruelty of solitary confinement and prompted British prison reform?
questions.explanation: Galsworthy's 1910 play 'Justice' depicted the destruction of clerk William Falder in prison, moving Winston Churchill to reform solitary confinement.

questions.question: Which Edwardian novelist set his major realist fiction, including 'Anna of the Five Towns' (1902), in the Staffordshire Potteries?
questions.explanation: Arnold Bennett, born in Hanley, Staffordshire, set his major realist novels in the industrial Potteries district known as the Five Towns.

questions.question: Which 1908 masterpiece by Arnold Bennett chronicles the contrasting lives of two sisters, Constance and Sophia Baines?
questions.explanation: Bennett's 1908 novel 'The Old Wives' Tale' traces sisters Constance and Sophia Baines from youth in Bursley to old age.

questions.question: Which 1910 novel by Arnold Bennett opened his acclaimed trilogy set in the Five Towns about a printer's son and Hilda Lessways?
questions.explanation: Bennett published 'Clayhanger' in 1910, followed by 'Hilda Lessways' in 1911 and 'These Twain' in 1916.

questions.question: Which 1909 novel by H. G. Wells satirizes Edwardian commercialism through the rise and fall of a fraudulent patent medicine?
questions.explanation: Wells's 1909 realist novel 'Tono-Bungay' critiques unregulated capitalism through Uncle Edward Ponderevo's quack tonic empire.

questions.question: Which two Edwardian comic novels by H. G. Wells (1905 and 1910) sympathetically portray frustrated lower-middle-class shopmen?
options: 'The Island of Doctor Moreau' and 'The Sea Lady'
'The First Men in the Moon' and 'The Sleeper Awakes'
questions.explanation: Wells drew on his own early drapery apprenticeship for his comic social novels 'Kipps' in 1905 and 'The History of Mr. Polly' in 1910.

questions.question: Which 1909 feminist novel by H. G. Wells depicts a rebellious young woman who leaves her suburban father's home to study biology?
questions.explanation: Wells's 1909 novel 'Ann Veronica' caused a sensation for portraying an independent New Woman and suffragette.

questions.question: Which Polish-born merchant mariner (born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski) became a preeminent Edwardian and early Modernist novelist?
questions.explanation: Joseph Conrad, born in Polish Ukraine, learned English as his third language and wrote masterpieces of early 20th-century fiction.

questions.question: In Joseph Conrad's novella 'Heart of Darkness' (published in book form in 1902), what are the famous final words of Mr. Kurtz?
options: 'Only connect the prose and the passion!'
questions.explanation: In Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness', narrated by Marlow along the Congo River, the dying ivory agent Kurtz cries The horror! The horror!

questions.question: Which 1904 political novel by Joseph Conrad is set in the fictional South American republic of Costaguana and centres on a silver mine?
questions.explanation: Conrad's 1904 novel 'Nostromo: A Tale of the Seaboard' examines imperialism and corruption around the San Tomé silver mine.

questions.question: Which 1907 novel by Joseph Conrad deals with anarchists, double agents, and an attempted bombing of the Greenwich Observatory?
questions.explanation: Conrad's 1907 ironic masterpiece 'The Secret Agent' is set in London's underworld of espionage and political extremism.

questions.question: Which Edwardian novelist critiqued English middle-class emotional repression in 'Where Angels Fear to Tread' (1905) and 'A Room with a View' (1908)?
questions.explanation: E. M. Forster contrasted restrictive English suburban norms with Italian spontaneity in his 1905 and 1908 novels.

questions.question: Which 1910 novel by E. M. Forster examines class and culture in Edwardian England under the famous epigraph 'Only connect...'?
questions.explanation: Forster's 1910 masterpiece 'Howards End' carries the epigraph Only connect, exploring the Schlegel, Wilcox, and Bast families.

questions.question: In E. M. Forster's 'A Room with a View' (1908), which young heroine rejects the pretentious Cecil Vyse to marry George Emerson?
questions.explanation: In Forster's 'A Room with a View', Lucy Honeychurch awakens to passion in Florence and marries George Emerson.

questions.question: Which author became the first English-language writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907?
questions.explanation: Rudyard Kipling was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, becoming the first British recipient of the honour.

questions.question: Which 1901 picaresque novel by Rudyard Kipling follows the orphaned Irish boy Kimball O'Hara and a Tibetan Lama across India?
questions.explanation: Kipling published 'Kim' in 1901, depicting Kim's spiritual bond with the Teshoo Lama and espionage in the Great Game.

questions.question: Which 1902 children's book by Rudyard Kipling tells playful origin stories such as 'How the Camel Got His Hump'?
questions.explanation: Kipling published 'Just So Stories for Little Children' in 1902, illustrated by himself.

questions.question: Which famous poem by Rudyard Kipling, published in 'Rewards and Fairies' (1910), outlines stoic virtues and ends 'you'll be a Man, my son!'?
questions.explanation: Kipling's poem 'If—', inspired by Leander Starr Jameson, appeared in 'Rewards and Fairies' in 1910.

questions.question: Which Edwardian writer created the intuitive Roman Catholic priest-detective Father Brown in 'The Innocence of Father Brown' (1911)?
questions.explanation: G. K. Chesterton introduced his priest-sleuth Father Brown in 'The Innocence of Father Brown' in 1911, followed by 'The Wisdom of Father Brown' in 1914.

questions.question: Who authored the 1908 metaphysical thriller 'The Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare', featuring the poet Gabriel Syme?
questions.explanation: Chesterton published 'The Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare' in 1908, allegorizing philosophical anarchy and cosmic order.

questions.question: Which Scottish dramatist wrote 'Peter Pan; or, The Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up', first performed in London in December 1904?
questions.explanation: J. M. Barrie's play 'Peter Pan', inspired by the Llewellyn Davies boys, premiered in London on 27 December 1904.

questions.question: In J. M. Barrie's 'Peter Pan' (1904), what is the name of the fantastical island home of Peter Pan, the Lost Boys, and Captain Hook?
questions.explanation: In Barrie's 'Peter Pan', Wendy, John, and Michael Darling fly with Peter Pan and Tinker Bell to Neverland.

questions.question: Which 1902 comic play by J. M. Barrie satirizes the British class system when a butler becomes leader of his shipwrecked employers?
questions.explanation: In Barrie's 1902 comedy 'The Admirable Crichton', Lord Loam's butler Crichton becomes the natural ruler on a desert island.

questions.question: Which 1908 children's classic by Kenneth Grahame chronicles the riverbank adventures of Mole, Water Rat, Badger, and Mr. Toad?
questions.explanation: Kenneth Grahame published 'The Wind in the Willows' in 1908 upon retiring from the Bank of England.

questions.question: Who wrote and illustrated the classic children's picture book 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit', commercially published by Frederick Warne in 1902?
questions.explanation: Beatrix Potter published 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit' in 1902, launching her celebrated series of children's tales.

questions.question: Which Edwardian author of children's literature wrote 'Five Children and It' (1902) and 'The Railway Children' (1906)?
questions.explanation: Edith Nesbit, a co-founder of the Fabian Society, wrote the Edwardian children's classics 'Five Children and It' and 'The Railway Children'.

questions.question: Which 1902 detective novel by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle features Sherlock Holmes investigating a diabolical family curse on Dartmoor?
questions.explanation: Conan Doyle serialized and published 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' in 1901–1902, reviving Sherlock Holmes before 'The Return of Sherlock Holmes' in 1905.

questions.question: Which national theatre was opened in Dublin in December 1904 by W. B. Yeats and Lady Gregory as the home of the Irish Literary Revival?
questions.explanation: Founded by W. B. Yeats and Lady Gregory with Annie Horniman's backing, Dublin's Abbey Theatre opened on 27 December 1904.

questions.question: Which Irish dramatist wrote the one-act Aran Islands tragedy 'Riders to the Sea' (1904) and 'The Playboy of the Western World' (1907)?
questions.explanation: J. M. Synge served as co-director of the Abbey Theatre and wrote 'Riders to the Sea' and 'The Playboy of the Western World'.

questions.question: Which author published the monumental three-part Napoleonic epic verse drama 'The Dynasts' between 1904 and 1908?
questions.explanation: Having abandoned novel-writing after 'Jude the Obscure', Thomas Hardy published his epic drama 'The Dynasts' in 1904, 1906, and 1908.

questions.question: Which scholar published the influential 1904 critical volume 'Shakespearean Tragedy', analyzing 'Hamlet', 'Othello', 'King Lear', and 'Macbeth'?
questions.explanation: A. C. Bradley's 'Shakespearean Tragedy' of 1904 is the most famous work of Edwardian Shakespeare criticism.

questions.question: Which poet published his debut collection 'Salt-Water Ballads' in 1902, including the famous poem 'Sea-Fever'?
questions.explanation: John Masefield drew on his merchant-marine youth for 'Salt-Water Ballads' in 1902 and later became Poet Laureate in 1930.

questions.question: What title was given to the popular series of poetry anthologies edited by Sir Edward Marsh beginning in 1912?
questions.explanation: Edward Marsh and Rupert Brooke launched 'Georgian Poetry' in 1912 to mark the new reign of King George V.

questions.question: Which Anglo-American poetic movement, launched around 1912 by Ezra Pound, H.D., and Richard Aldington, championed clear, hard visual images?
questions.explanation: Imagism rejected Victorian sentimentality in favour of free-verse cadence, economy of language, and concrete imagery.

questions.question: Which semi-autobiographical 1913 novel by D. H. Lawrence portrays Paul Morel and his working-class coal-mining family in Nottinghamshire?
questions.explanation: D. H. Lawrence published his breakthrough autobiographical novel 'Sons and Lovers' in 1913.

questions.question: Which landmark collection of fifteen short stories by James Joyce, depicting the 'paralysis' of Irish urban life, was published in June 1914?
questions.explanation: James Joyce published 'Dubliners' in June 1914, culminating in the novella-length story 'The Dead'.

questions.question: Which American-born expatriate novelist published 'The Wings of the Dove' (1902), 'The Ambassadors' (1903), and 'The Golden Bowl' (1904)?
questions.explanation: Henry James lived in England and crowned his career with his three great late novels between 1902 and 1904.

questions.question: Under which pen name did Hector Hugh Munro (1870–1916) write his satirical Edwardian short-story collections 'Reginald' (1904) and 'Beasts and Super-Beasts' (1914)?
questions.explanation: H. H. Munro used the pen name Saki, borrowed from the cupbearer in the 'Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam', for his witty Edwardian tales.

questions.question: Which circle of writers, critics, and artists—including Virginia Stephen (Woolf), Lytton Strachey, and E. M. Forster—formed in London around 1905?
questions.explanation: The Bloomsbury Group met in the Bloomsbury district of London from about 1905, championing aesthetic freedom and modernism.

questions.question: Which militant women's suffrage organization was founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst under the motto 'Deeds, not words'?
options: The Women's Social and Political Union
questions.explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the WSPU in 1903, leading the militant Edwardian Suffragette campaign for women's voting rights.

questions.question: Which April 1912 maritime disaster inspired Thomas Hardy's famous philosophical poem 'The Convergence of the Twain'?
options: The sinking of the RMS Titanic
The mutiny on the HMS Bounty
The torpedoing of the RMS Lusitania
questions.explanation: Hardy wrote 'The Convergence of the Twain: Lines on the Loss of the Titanic' after the liner sank on 15 April 1912.
